angle: Fix the output not the input: level/shape decomposition, regional duration curves, hierarchical pooling
verdict: PURSUE ONLY AS A CHEAP DIAGNOSTIC AND ONE NARROW EXPERIMENT; DO NOT ADOPT THE MACHINERY. The verified evidence for this angle is thin, entirely from streamflow (not water quality), and points the wrong way for our deployment target. Three findings drive the verdict. (1) The decomposition RELOCATES our problem rather than solving it: QPPQ and its copula generalization split prediction into a donor-borrowed timing channel (which we already do well, within_r2 0.42 / macro_auc 0.90) and a site-specific marginal / duration curve carrying the absolute level (which is exactly our failing between_r2 0.21 term). Adopting it concentrates 100% of the residual error into the term we cannot currently estimate, and NONE of the verified sources supplies a method for regionalizing that marginal from attributes at our sample size. (2) The one verified benchmark in the ungauged regime is a NULL: Worland et al. (2019, WRR 55:9378-9397, doi:10.1029/2019WR025138) report that copula/duration-curve machinery is only 'competitive albeit nondominating' for ungaged sites once realistic estimation error enters the FDCs AND the inter-site correlations; its wins are confined to the perfect-information limit and to partially gaged sites with several years of the target's own record - two regimes an arbitrary Iowa map pin can never occupy. (3) The single paper that DID attempt pure attribute-to-distribution regionalization (Worland et al. 2019, WRR 55:6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463, multioutput neural network -> FDC quantiles) was REFUTED on protocol during verification: the authors' own code performs random 10-fold CV over rows of a site-decade table with no grouping by site_no, so the same gage appears in train and test in different decades. That is precisely the leakage our 19-family CV exists to prevent, and it means the literature's flagship attribute-to-duration-curve result carries no ungauged-transfer evidence at all. Worse, that paper's own verified directional finding is a negative for us: static basin characteristics were most informative for the LOW quantiles, while the HIGH quantiles were driven by neighboring-quantile bias terms - and our target (violation = daily max >= 10 mg/L, top ~26%) is an upper-tail exceedance. WHAT IS ACTUALLY WORTH DOING, in priority order. (a) FREE, ADOPT IMMEDIATELY: a hard evaluation rule - if any level/shape or concentration-duration-curve decomposition is trialled, the CDC must be ESTIMATED FROM STATIC ATTRIBUTES under LOFO; the observed-CDC-plugged-in variant may be reported only as an explicitly labelled diagnostic CEILING. Plugging in the target's observed CDC hands the model the answer to the between-site problem and will manufacture a fake gain. (b) ONE GENUINELY NEW, DEPLOYMENT-COMPATIBLE EXPERIMENT: our rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5 features are a statewide scalar mean - the degenerate collapse of a QPPQ donor channel. The copula formalism says the donor channel should be per-donor and similarity-weighted. Replacing the statewide mean with k-nearest-monitored-site nonexceedance transfer (donor nitrate percentiles weighted by inter-site rank correlation or attribute/distance similarity) uses OTHER sites' observations, never the target's, so it is deployment-legal at an arbitrary pin. This is a new feature the project does not have, not a restatement of the existing one. Expect it to improve the TIMING channel, which is not our bottleneck - so treat it as a moderate-value side bet, not the fix. (c) THE ANGLE'S MOST VALUABLE OUTPUT IS ACTUALLY AN INPUT LEAD, which is an honest admission that 'fix the output not the input' is the wrong framing here. Every duration-curve source that names the predictors carrying the LEVEL names SUBSURFACE and GEOLOGIC descriptors - baseflow index, permeability, topographic wetness, soil drainage class, depth to water table - none of which are in our 68 features. The refutation of the MNN paper surfaced the authors' full NHDPlus-accumulated attribute inventory (bfi, twi, soller surficial geology, bedperm, aquifers, hlr, physio, strm_dens, sinuosity, flood_storage), free and CONUS-wide so it covers our multi-state basin portions. That is the concrete, actionable deliverable of this angle. WHAT TO REJECT OUTRIGHT: do not build QPPQ/copula transfer (requires a concurrently-gauged donor AND a target FDC; 0 of our 61 IWQIS sites have discharge). Do not build load-duration curves (an LDC requires a daily discharge series at the target to place each day on the FDC, and EPA's own guidance shows that when the target concentration is flow-invariant - which it is for nitrate at 10 mg/L - LDC exceedance is mathematically IDENTICAL to concentration >= 10 mg/L, so the LDC adds zero predictive information over the label we already have). Do not plan on quantile mapping or a fitted site random intercept at the deployment pin: with zero observations there is no local sample to map from, which is arithmetic, not a research question. FINALLY, THE BIGGEST GAP: the assignment asked specifically about hierarchical/partial-pooling models with attribute-predicted site random effects, quantile regression forests / distributional GBDT, and domain adaptation. The corpus returned NOTHING VERIFIABLE on any of the three - not one paper, not even at tier 3, and the canonical IAHS duration-curve synthesis was reported (unverified) to contain zero hierarchical-Bayes, zero random-effect and zero quantile-regression-forest work. Those three sub-questions are UNRESEARCHED, not answered in the negative, and the partial-pooling branch in particular remains the most plausible untested route to a between-site level term at n=19. It should be re-run as its own search before this angle is closed.

findings.claim: STRUCTURAL, AND THE CENTRAL REASON THIS ANGLE UNDERDELIVERS: the QPPQ framework decomposes a prediction into exactly the two pieces this project wants separated - (a) a duration curve / marginal distribution at the target, which carries the absolute LEVEL, and (b) a time series of nonexceedance probabilities borrowed from donor gauges, which carries the TIMING. Worland et al. state it directly: 'FDC-based streamflow estimation methods involve estimating an FDC at an ungaged or partially gaged location and using the time series of nonexceedance probabilities estimated from donor streamgage sites to generate estimates of streamflow.' The consequence for us is the opposite of encouraging: because our model is already a good timer and a bad site-ranker, adopting this decomposition moves essentially ALL remaining error into component (a), the site marginal - which IS the between_r2 0.21 / between_rate_r2 0.24 term we are failing at - and the paper supplies no method for estimating that marginal from static attributes. The decomposition isolates the problem; it does not solve it. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: QPPQ predates this paper (Fennessey 1994; Hughes & Smakhtin 1996; Archfield & Vogel 2010); Worland et al. generalize it via copulas rather than defining it.

findings.feasibilityAtN19: The decomposition itself is free to adopt at any n - it is a way of organizing the prediction, not a fitted model. But the half it hands you to solve (regressing duration-curve parameters on basin attributes) is a ~19-point regression, which is where the whole angle stalls.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: PARTIALLY. Component (b), the donor channel, is deployment-legal because it uses other sites' observations - we already have a crude version in rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1. Component (a), the target's own duration curve, is NOT available at an arbitrary pin and must be regionalized from attributes, which no verified source here demonstrates for water quality.

findings.claim: VERIFIED NULL RESULT IN EXACTLY OUR REGIME. The paper's own headline finding, quoted verbatim from the abstract, is that copula approaches '(4) remain a competitive albeit nondominating method for ungaged sites and partially gaged sites with limited data when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network.' Their reported wins are confined to '(1) the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs across the gaging network' and '(3) partially gaged sites with several years of available data' - both of which require either target-site observations or network information we do not have. TWO CORRECTIONS APPLIED BY VERIFIERS: first, the advantage DEGRADES TO PARITY, it does not reverse - no competing method is reported to overtake copulas, and the abstract separately credits copulas with '(2) provid[ing] a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative', so they are described as relatively MORE robust as information degrades. Do not report this as a 'ranking reversal'. Second, the loss of dominance is attributed jointly to estimation error in the FDCs AND in the inter-site correlations; the abstract never decomposes which one binds, so it is wrong to conclude 'the duration curve is the binding constraint, not the dependence model'. The correct, weaker statement: the limiting factor is the REGIONALIZATION STEP AS A WHOLE. For an arbitrary Iowa pin we have realistic error in both inputs simultaneously - squarely the regime where the authors report the sophisticated machinery stops paying for itself.
findings.effectSize: Qualitative only. 'Competitive albeit nondominating' at ungaged sites; 'outperform other methods' at partially gaged sites with several years of local data. No NSE/KGE/RMSE magnitudes are recoverable from any free route - Wiley returns HTTP 403 (Cloudflare bot challenge, cf-mitigated: challenge) on the landing page, /full, /epdf, /pdfdirect and /full-xml despite a CC-BY license, and OpenAlex lists exactly one OA location (the blocked Wiley PDF) with no repository mirror anywhere in the OA graph.

As evidence it is unusually sample-size-relevant precisely because it is small - but see the next finding: 74 raw gages in 2 nested networks would collapse well below 19 under our own leak-safe grouping rule, so this is not a small-n existence proof either.

Only the null result transfers, as a reason not to invest.

findings.claim: REFUTED-ON-PROTOCOL, BUT ITS DIRECTIONAL FINDING IS A VERIFIED NEGATIVE FOR US. Worland et al. (2019, WRR 55(8):6850-6868, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463) is the flagship pure attribute-to-distribution regionalization study - a multioutput neural network taking static basin characteristics and emitting all FDC quantiles simultaneously, applied to 9,203 ungaged HUC12 pour points in the southeastern US for six decades (1950-2009), with a combined loss enforcing monotonically increasing quantiles and prediction-time dropout for posterior-predictive bands. Structurally this is precisely what an Iowa concentration-duration-curve head would look like, and it needs no target-site data. BUT its validation is not a spatial holdout: the authors' own code (scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R, function sw_k_foldcv) does `N <- nrow(data); set.seed(1); indices <- sample(1:N); folds <- cut(indices, breaks = k, labels = FALSE)` - random 10-fold CV over ROWS of a site-decade table with no grouping by site_no. Each gage contributes up to 6 decade-rows with near-identical static attributes, so the same gage appears in train and test folds. The production model uses Keras validation_split=0.1 (last 10% of rows), also non-spatial. There is no held-out-ungaged evaluation anywhere in the workflow; the 9,203 pour-point predictions are unvalidated extrapolation. AND its verified abstract states a negative for our exact target: 'basin characteristics are most useful for predicting smaller quantiles, whereas bias terms from neighboring quantiles are most informative for predicting higher quantiles.' Our violation label is an UPPER-tail exceedance (daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263), i.e. the regime where this study found static attributes carry the LEAST information.
findings.effectSize: No NSE/RMSE/R2 is retrievable (Wiley 402/403; OpenAlex any_repository_has_fulltext: false). The only quantitative direction available is the negative one above. Two salvageable architecture facts: a single-output-per-quantile network produced 2,316 monotonicity violations after 400 epochs while the joint multioutput loss drove violations to zero by ~100 epochs (this specific figure is TIER 3 / unverified); the loss weighting in code is `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))`.
findings.splitProtocol: RANDOM ROW-WISE 10-FOLD CV WITH SAME-SITE LEAKAGE. Explicitly NOT a spatial holdout. Under this project's Rule 1, no number from this paper may be placed alongside our LOFO 0.820.
findings.nBasins: ~956 gages / 2,804-2,816 gage-decades (verified by downloading the authors' released tables: all_gage_covariates.csv = 5,736 rows x 48 cols, 956 unique site_no x 6 decades; all_gage_flow_stats.csv = 2,804 rows, 956 unique site_no; data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt states 962 gages with a complete decade out of 1,290 screened). The widely-circulated figure of 688 gages is unsourced and contradicted by the authors' own data release.

findings.feasibilityAtN19: INFEASIBLE AS PUBLISHED. The architecture is ~40 inputs -> dense 28 -> dropout 0.27 -> dense 40 -> dropout 0.70 -> 27 linear quantile heads, on the order of 2,500+ parameters, trained on ~2,804 gage-decade rows. Our 19 independent basin families is ~50x smaller than the gage count and ~150x smaller than the row count. A drastically reduced version (a handful of quantile heads, strong regularization, or a monotone GBDT with a shared trunk) is the only conceivable port, and would be an unevidenced experiment.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES structurally - the input side is attribute-only, requiring no local observations, no gauged neighbour and no discharge at the target. That is the one genuinely useful property. But it is also the trivial part: our current model is already attribute-plus-weather with no local history, so the paper offers architecture without evidence.

findings.claim: THE ONE PIECE OF RECOMPUTED NUMERIC EVIDENCE, AND WHY IT STILL DOES NOT HELP. Although the Worland et al. (2019) copula paper's full text is unreachable, its companion USGS data release (doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU, ScienceBase item 5cae0b6ce4b0c3b006549e61) is fully public and ships observed values plus all 16 method predictions for 270,322 site-days (74 gages x 3,653 days). Recomputing method-level skill directly from that archive gives median per-site NSE of 0.779 for the multivariate Gaussian copula, 0.657 for the best QPPQ variant, and 0.565 for the best drainage-area-ratio variant. CRITICAL CAVEAT THAT NEUTRALIZES THESE NUMBERS FOR US: reading sb_functions.R shows the shipped configuration is the PARTIALLY GAGED case, not the ungaged one. Seven of the 16 methods (QPPQ_nearest_neighbor, QPPQ_highest_rho, QPPQ_IDW, QPPQ_mu, bivar_cop_nn, bivar_cop_rho, multivar_norm_cop) invert through `quantile(R[,i], ...)` - the TARGET SITE'S OWN empirical flow-duration curve - and use empirical correlations computed from the target's own record (`sigma[i,-i]`); the donor-selection step also picks the highest-correlation donor using observed target correlations. The leak-free variant requires the optional loo_krige_cor() kriging step plus externally regionalized FDCs from a second release (doi:10.5066/P9YGKZZV). So these NSE figures describe a regime our product can never occupy, and the genuinely ungaged performance figures are absent from the archive. GENERAL LESSON WORTH KEEPING: when a publisher blocks a paper, resolve the companion USGS/ScienceBase data-release DOI with curl and a browser User-Agent before declaring the numbers unavailable.
findings.effectSize: Median per-site NSE: multivariate Gaussian copula 0.779 > best QPPQ 0.657 > best drainage-area-ratio 0.565 (recomputed from the data release, PARTIALLY-GAGED configuration). Reported by one verifier only; two other verifiers independently concluded no numbers were extractable, so treat as recomputed-not-published and confirm before citing.

findings.feasibilityAtN19: Not portable. Only 9 of the 16 methods are genuinely ungaged-capable (DAR, IDW, correlation-weighted and averaging variants), and all 9 still require a gauged donor with a concurrent time series. Note also that the 74 gages are heavily nested and cross-correlated (Mobile-Tombigbee median pairwise Spearman rho 0.774, 42% of pairs above 0.8, max 0.984), with basin areas spanning ~15.7 to ~47,698 km2 inside two HUC4s - applying our own nesting rule would collapse 74 to well below 19. This is not a small-n success story.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO. The configuration that produced these numbers requires the target's own 10-year record.

findings.claim: HARD EVALUATION RULE, ADOPT REGARDLESS OF WHETHER THE ANGLE IS PURSUED. Worland et al. condition all results on an information-quality regime rather than reporting a single number: dominance under 'the limiting case of perfect information with regard to the rank-based correlation structure and FDCs', degrading to non-dominance once 'realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network'. The operational implication for this project: ANY measured gain from a level/shape or concentration-duration-curve decomposition MUST be evaluated with the CDC estimated from STATIC ATTRIBUTES under LOFO. Plugging in the target site's OBSERVED CDC is the perfect-information regime and will manufacture a spurious gain, because a site's observed CDC encodes exactly the between-site absolute level the model is failing at - it hands the model the answer to the between_r2 = 0.21 problem, in the same way a random split over autocorrelated site-days manufactures apparent transfer skill. If both are reported, label the observed-CDC variant explicitly as a DIAGNOSTIC CEILING, never as a result. ATTRIBUTION HONESTY: this rule follows from the project's own Rule 1, not from Worland et al.; the paper's contribution is empirical precedent from a neighbouring domain that the perfect-information regime does not merely inflate a number but changes which method appears best. The extension from streamflow FDCs to nitrate CDCs is our analogy, not the paper's. Expect the perfect-information / realistic-error gap to be LARGER here than in their 74-site network, because an attribute-estimated CDC fitted over 19 families will be noisier.

findings.claim: CONCRETE, DEPLOYMENT-LEGAL EXPERIMENT THAT THIS ANGLE ACTUALLY MOTIVATES: upgrade the donor channel. Our rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5 features are a single statewide scalar mean, identical for every target pin - which is the DEGENERATE COLLAPSE of a QPPQ/copula donor channel, not an implementation of one. The copula formalism requires component (b) to be per-donor and similarity-weighted, with a rank correlation that decays with separation. Read properly, the paper suggests REPLACING the statewide mean with distance- and attribute-weighted donor selection (a k-nearest-monitored-site nonexceedance transfer over the ~85-sensor network), not preserving it. This is a new feature the project does not have. It is deployment-legal because it consumes OTHER sites' concurrent observations and never the target's - exactly the property that makes it usable at an arbitrary pin, and exactly what distinguishes it from quantile mapping. TEMPER EXPECTATIONS: this improves the TIMING channel, which is already our strong term (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90). It does not address the between-site level. Also note a domain risk the source cannot settle: streamflow has strong, slowly-decaying inter-site rank correlation, which is what makes donor transfer work; nitrate rank correlation between Iowa basins is driven by local N application and tile hydrology and plausibly decays much faster. Measure the empirical inter-site nitrate rank-correlation-versus-distance curve across the 85 sensors FIRST - it is a cheap precondition test, and if correlation decays fast the whole donor idea is dead before any feature is built.
findings.effectSize: No effect size exists for this proposal. The source supports the ARCHITECTURE, never a predicted gain.
findings.splitProtocol: Must be evaluated under our existing LOFO leave-one-basin-family-out.
findings.nBasins: n/a - proposal. Donor pool would be our ~85 nitrate sensors (all 85 are usable as nitrate donors, unlike the discharge case where only 22 are gauged).
sources: Worland et al. (2019), WRR 55(11):9378-9397, doi:10.1029/2019WR025138 (donor-channel formalism; verified from abstract + archived code sb_functions.R)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Feasible with a caveat. The donor features themselves are cheap to build. But a full network-wide rank-correlation SURFACE is not identifiable at 19 independent families - use a simple parametric distance-decay or attribute-similarity weighting with 1-2 free parameters, not a kriged correlation field.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES - this is the rare item in this angle that does. It requires no observations at the target, only concurrent readings from the existing sensor network, which the shipped product can query in real time.

findings.claim: ARITHMETIC LIMIT ON THE POST-HOC CALIBRATION BRANCH, WHICH IS THE CRUX OF THE ASSIGNED QUESTION. Quantile mapping, per-site bias correction, and a FITTED site random intercept all require a local empirical sample to map from or shrink toward. At a deployment pin with ZERO observations that sample is empty, so these methods are unavailable by construction - not by weak evidence. They remain usable for the ~85 existing sensor sites and for any future site after multi-year monitoring, and that limitation must be stated prominently wherever they are proposed. IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION CORRECTION: an earlier version of this claim cited Worland et al.'s partially-gaged findings as a 'direct negative' establishing a years-scale data threshold. That inference was REFUTED during verification and must not be repeated - the paper's points (3) and (4) rank COPULAS AGAINST OTHER FDC-BASED METHODS within fixed information regimes; they say nothing about when a site's own observations begin to pay off in absolute terms, and are fully consistent with all methods gaining large absolute skill from a short local record. Moreover the fully-ungaged case is one of the paper's two headline regimes, not below its tested range, and 'competitive albeit nondominating' is a neutral-to-mildly-positive result for zero-observation regionalization, not a negative one. The deployment limitation is true, but it follows from the definition of the product, and citing Worland et al. as its authority is a misattribution. NOTE ALSO: the one path that IS estimable for a zero-observation pin - predicting duration-curve parameters from static basin attributes - is not a grudging residual; it is the paper's own ungaged method, and the paper reports that configuration as competitive.
sources: Project deployment definition (arbitrary map pin, no local nitrate history)
Refutation record for the Worland et al. 'several years' threshold inference
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Fitting a site random intercept for the 19 training families is feasible; the problem is not estimation but PREDICTION of that intercept at a new site, which requires regressing 19 intercepts on attributes.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO for quantile mapping and for any fitted-per-site intercept. The only zero-observation-compatible variant is predicting the intercept / duration-curve parameters FROM ATTRIBUTES, which is a ~19-point regression and is the unsolved core of this angle.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - the most quantitatively striking result for this angle, and it needs verification before it is used for anything. The IAHS/PUB synthesis chapter on predicting flow duration curves in ungauged basins is reported to quantify the level/shape split directly: pooling 1,419 catchments from 7 author groups across 4 regionalisation families (regression, index-flow, geostatistical, process-based), all leave-one-out cross-validated with each catchment treated as ungauged, 'R2 of the slope of the FDC were calculated for all methods in each study separately which gave a median of 0.26. Also the NSE of the quantiles of the scaled FDC were calculated which gave a median of 0.98.' Slope defined as (Q30% - Q70%)/40 in normalised runoff. If true, this is a near-exact structural analogue of our within_r2 0.42 versus between_r2 0.21 split: once the site-specific index flow is divided out, the dimensionless SHAPE transfers almost perfectly across ungauged sites, while the site-specific level/slope term is nearly unpredictable from attributes. THIS CLAIM IS UNVERIFIED and must not be used as the warrant for any recommendation - but as a lead it is the single most important thing in this corpus, because it would mean the between-site level problem is hard in the source literature too, and that our 0.21 is not obviously a fixable defect.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: median R2 = 0.26 for FDC slope (between-site term); median NSE = 0.98 for quantiles of the index-scaled FDC

findings.nBasins: reported as 1,419 catchments (Austria, France, Italy, USA), 7 contributing groups, 4 method families - unverified

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - the most damaging reported finding for this angle, if it holds. The same IAHS chapter is reported to conclude that a very short LOCAL record beats every regionalisation method: from Castellarin et al. (2004a) resampling experiments, 'predictions of long-term FDCs based upon five years of observed runoff largely outperform the best performing regional model, while one or two years of daily runoff are generally sufficient to obtain predictions of FDCs that are as accurate as the ones retrieved through regionalization', with the Level 1 synthesis reportedly stating 'Methods that use short runoff records at the site of interest perform better than any regionalisation method provided at least one year of daily runoff data is available'. The chapter is also reported to warn 'it is generally not advisable to rely completely on any regional model, which should be used to provide a first order approximation of FDCs.' IF VERIFIED, this says the duration-curve angle delivers its gains from LOCAL DATA - which the arbitrary-map-pin case does not have - and that zero-observation regionalization of the level is the WEAKEST branch of this literature, not the strong one. UNVERIFIED; do not use as the warrant for a decision. But it is the highest-value verification target in this angle, because if true it largely closes the question.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 1-2 years of local daily record approximately equals the best regional model; 5 years 'largely outperform' it; only 3 of 27 method-results in the meta-analysis were short-record methods
findings.nBasins: UNVERIFIED - underlying Castellarin et al. (2004a) resampling n not stated in the chapter; 3 short-record results within a 10-study set
sources: IAHS/PUB Chapter 7 PDF (Tufts mirror), https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.tufts.edu/dist/a/4406/files/2019/04/2013_predictionFlowDurationCurves.pdf - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
findings.feasibilityAtN19: n/a - it is an argument against the approach, not a method.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The finding is precisely that the well-performing option does NOT work at an ungauged pin.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - reported evidence that regionalisation skill scales with donor-pool size, which if true places our n=19 at the bottom of the usable range. The IAHS chapter is reported to state 'Figure 7.21 shows that performance increases with the number of catchments used in the analysis. The trend is particularly clear for the comparison ... for the intermediate classes of catchment number (from 20 to 250 catchments per study)', concluding 'even if one is interested in estimating a FDC for a single catchment it may be worth basing the regionalisation on a large number of catchments', with the lowest catchment-count bin (below 20) reportedly the worst-performing. It reportedly attributes the index method's weaker showing in Italy to 'the lower stream gauge density' versus Austria and France which 'both have a relatively dense stream gauge network'. Separately reported: across a Level 1 meta-analysis of 13 studies (10 usable, all leave-one-out, 27 method-results), per-study catchment counts ranged 8 to 1,080 with a MEDIAN OF 49, and back-calculated NSE of FDC quantiles had 25th and 75th percentiles of 0.60 and 0.90. UNVERIFIED. Two readings cut against each other and both should be held: the median study size of 49 shows this literature is NOT dominated by CAMELS-scale datasets, so it is more sample-size-relevant to us than the deep-learning literature; but the donor-count trend says 19 sits at or below the bottom of the range where usable skill is reported.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: monotone improvement across catchment-count strata (<20, 20-250, >250); NSE of FDC quantiles 25th pct 0.60 / 75th pct 0.90 across 27 method-results
findings.splitProtocol: reported as spatial holdout (all retained studies performed leave-one-out CV) - unverified
findings.nBasins: UNVERIFIED: 13 studies screened, 10 used; per-study n 8 to 1,080, median 49; Level 2 pooled 1,419
sources: IAHS/PUB Chapter 7 PDF (Tufts mirror) - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
findings.feasibilityAtN19: This IS the n=19 finding, if it verifies. It would predict degraded but not necessarily zero skill; the smallest reported study was 8 catchments.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: n/a - concerns the donor pool size, not the target's data.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - the closest thing in the corpus to a small-n attribute-to-duration-curve-shape result, and a useful LEAD for a cheap experiment. Kamrath & Yuan (2023, J. Environ. Manage. 336:117598, doi:10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598) reportedly partitioned daily nutrient loads by flow-duration-curve interval across 14 gauged Ohio watersheds (11 to 16,388 km2, 2000-2020, 3 to 21 years each) and regressed the resulting load-shape parameter on just two static attributes: m10% (percent of annual load in the top-10% flow interval) = b0 + b1*log(watershed area) + b2*(percent agricultural land), n=13 after removing Cuyahoga as an outlier, reported adjusted R2 = 0.86, F(2,10) = 37.7, p < 0.001, b1 = -4.24, b2 = +1.1; the 10-40th percentile interval reportedly gave adjusted R2 = 0.71. Direction: LARGER basins concentrate LESS load in high flows, MORE agricultural basins concentrate MORE. THE R2 IS REPORTEDLY IN-SAMPLE WITH NO CROSS-VALIDATION, NO HOLDOUT AND NO LEAVE-ONE-WATERSHED-OUT TEST (13 observations, 3 fitted parameters, 10 residual df), so it is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 and is very likely optimistic. ALL OF THIS IS UNVERIFIED and cannot warrant a recommendation. Its value is as a lead: it suggests that a per-site distributional SHAPE parameter may be regressable on 2 static attributes at a sample size of the same order as our 19 families - and both attributes (log_basin_area, CDL crop fractions) are already in our feature set, which would imply our between-site deficit comes from not ASKING the model to predict a site-level shape parameter rather than from missing these two inputs. Reportedly also: Mann-Kendall tests found no significant temporal trend in the load-shape partition at any site over 2000-2020, supporting treatment of the shape as a static per-site property. Reportedly the paper attempts NO ungauged prediction, builds no concentration-duration curves, and does not consider basin length, slope, shape or drainage density.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED and IN-SAMPLE: adj R2 = 0.86 (m10% NO3-N), adj R2 = 0.71 (10-40th pct interval), n = 13, 2 predictors. Also reported: median 58% of annual NO3-N load in the top 10% of flow days, 93% in the top 40%, cross-watershed range 20-96%.
findings.splitProtocol: IN-SAMPLE, no holdout, no cross-validation reported - explicitly NOT comparable to any spatially held-out number
findings.nBasins: 14 gauged Ohio watersheds (western Lake Erie + Mississippi basins); 13 in the regression
sources: Kamrath & Yuan (2023), J. Environ. Manage. 336:117598, doi:10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.117598, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10168011/ - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
findings.feasibilityAtN19: This is the one reported precedent at a comparable n (13). If verified, it would be the strongest available argument that an attribute-driven regionalization of a DISTRIBUTIONAL SHAPE parameter (as opposed to a per-day time series) is statistically feasible at our sample size. Caveat: an in-sample adj R2 at n=13 with 2 predictors has very wide uncertainty and no out-of-sample confirmation.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO as published. Every load-duration curve in the study requires a measured daily discharge record at the site to place each day on the flow-duration curve, and the paper performs zero ungauged predictions. Our project has discharge at 22 of 85 sites and none at an arbitrary pin.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) BUT DECISIVE IF TRUE - the load-duration-curve branch may add literally nothing predictive for our label. EPA's official duration-curve guidance (EPA 841-B-07-006) reportedly constructs a load duration curve as Load = Flow (cfs) x target concentration (mg/L) x conversion factor, and reportedly lists nitrate among the pollutants whose numeric target 'may be constant across all flow conditions', with its worked nitrate example (Figure 2-1; Appendix B Figure B-2, Sangamon River) using the drinking-water MCL of 10 mg/L - IDENTICAL to this project's violation threshold. If the target concentration is flow-invariant, then exceeding the LDC is mathematically identical to concentration >= 10 mg/L: the flow multiplies both sides. The LDC would therefore add NO information beyond the label we already have, and its value would be purely diagnostic (WHICH flow zone exceedances fall in), not predictive. This is a strong reason to deprioritize the LDC branch, but it is UNVERIFIED and rests on a tier-3 reading of the guidance; confirm the flow-invariance statement before acting on it. Reportedly the same document also (a) acknowledges the ungauged problem in only two sentences, naming similar-waterbody regression, drainage-area ratios and rainfall-runoff models, with ZERO accuracy, bias or validation numbers attached to any of them anywhere in its 74 pages; and (b) states an applicability limit directly threatening this pollutant: 'The duration curve alone does not consider specific fate and transport mechanisms ... plant uptake of nutrients, or chemical transformations', and is 'more appropriate in cases where flow is a primary driver in pollutant delivery mechanisms'. Iowa nitrate is modulated by N application, crop rotation, denitrification and tile routing, so EPA's own criterion flags a pure flow-duration framework as a partial tool here.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: no skill statistic of any kind is reported anywhere in the document - it is prescriptive guidance, not a validation study. The only numeric quality bar reported is an r-squared >= 0.25 acceptance floor for index-gauge regression in the South Carolina Pee Dee case study, with a 150 km search radius and >= 300 matching daily observations.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable (no validation performed; record infilling only, no held-out evaluation)
sources: US EPA (2007), 'An Approach for Using Load Duration Curves in the Development of TMDLs', EPA 841-B-07-006, https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-07/documents/2007_08_23_tmdl_duration_curve_guide_aug2007.pdf - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
findings.feasibilityAtN19: n/a - the framework is not a fitted model. Its five-zone partition (0-10% high, 10-40% moist, 40-60% mid, 60-90% dry, 90-100% low) is a coarse, low-degree-of-freedom shape representation that would be attractive at n=19, but it requires a flow percentile at the target that we cannot compute.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO. An LDC is defined on top of a flow-duration curve at the site of interest, so it cannot produce a concentration prediction without a daily discharge estimate at the target. Using it would require first solving ungauged flow regionalization, for which this document provides no validated method and no error estimate.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - a LEAD pointing away from this angle and toward missing static inputs. Two reported precedents converge on subsurface-pathway descriptors as the controls on between-site nitrate level. (a) Nolan, Hitt & Ruddy (2002, Environ. Sci. Technol. 36(10):2138-2145, doi:10.1021/es0113854), as summarized in a secondary source, reportedly fit a logistic regression for probability of nitrate exceedance (>4 mg N/L) in recently recharged shallow groundwater across the conterminous USA, 'calibrated on 1280 observations, predicted the correct status of nitrate concentration in 75% of the 736 verification observations', with six significant predictors: N fertilizer loading, % cropland-pasture, ln(population density), % well-drained soils, depth to seasonally high water table, and presence of unconsolidated sand-and-gravel aquifers - which the authors reportedly partition explicitly as 'Predictors 4-6 relate to the hydrological pathway and time of travel, whereas predictors 1-3 relate to the source of the nitrate.' HALF the predictors are subsurface drainage-pathway descriptors, none of which exist in our 68 features. (b) McLay et al. (2001, Environ. Pollut. 115(2):191-204), as summarized in the same source, reportedly assessed groundwater nitrate at 88 New Zealand sites and found 'no discernible trends' from dominant land use, with a risk model explaining only ~50% of concentration variance and 'the permeability of the vadose zone being the most important parameter'; associations emerged only for fine-grained operation types, not coarse land-use class. BOTH UNVERIFIED. Caveats even if verified: both are groundwater, not stream nitrate; the 75% accuracy is against an unstated base rate and is NOT comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820; McLay's ~50% is apparently in-sample. As a LEAD, though, this is the corpus's most consistent signal - and it argues that the fix for between_r2 0.21 is a missing INPUT class (subsurface permeability, soil drainage class, depth to water table, baseflow index, tile drainage), not a reorganized OUTPUT.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: 75% correct exceedance status on 736 held-out verification observations (Nolan et al.); ~50% of site-level nitrate variance explained, vadose-zone permeability the top parameter (McLay et al.)
findings.splitProtocol: unknown for both - spatial independence of Nolan's 736-observation verification set is not stated in the summary; McLay's figure appears to be in-sample variance explained
findings.nBasins: Nolan: 1,280 calibration + 736 verification observations (wells, not basins). McLay: 88 sites.
sources: Peters, Reynolds & Johnes (2007), IAHS Publ. 309:63-73, https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/1778/1/001778Peters.pdf (secondary summary source) - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
Primary sources not retrieved: Nolan, Hitt & Ruddy (2002), doi:10.1021/es0113854; McLay et al. (2001), Environ. Pollut. 115(2):191-204
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Nolan's design is a 1,280-observation regression, ~67x our 19 families. McLay's 88 sites is ~4.6x. Neither certifies the approach at n=19, but both use small fixed predictor sets (6 and fewer), which is the right shape for a low-n regression - unlike a 40-input neural network.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES in principle - both are attribute-only classifications/regressions requiring no local observations at the prediction location. That is what makes this the most deployment-compatible lead in the corpus, and why it should be routed to the feature-acquisition workstream rather than this one.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED (TIER 3) - a reported structural argument that our chosen target is the hardest point on the aggregation curve, plus a cheap fallback worth measuring. Peters, Reynolds & Johnes (2007, IAHS Publ. 309:63-73) reportedly conclude that 'uncertainty of the estimates of average constituent concentration or yield decreases with increasing averaging time, e.g. a predicted annual flux is more precise than an instantaneous or daily flux', closing with 'Although we may adequately predict average conditions (chronic), we may fail to predict biologically important extremes (acute).' If verified, this asserts that (i) the ungauged water-quality literature's reported skill is overwhelmingly for ANNUAL fluxes and is therefore NOT comparable to a daily-violation AUC, and (ii) a level/shape decomposition in which the 'level' is a LONG-AVERAGING-TIME quantity - e.g. predicting a per-basin annual or seasonal exceedance FREQUENCY - should be materially more accurate than predicting individual site-days. That second point is a concrete, cheap, deployment-legal experiment: compute each family's observed annual violation rate, regress it on static attributes under LOFO, and see whether between-family rate prediction improves over the current between_rate_r2 0.24. It costs nothing beyond existing data. UNVERIFIED. Note also the verified negative about this same source recorded under refuted[]: it contains ZERO mention of QPPQ, duration curves, quantile mapping, hierarchical pooling or domain adaptation, so it must not be cited as support for the duration-curve angle itself.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED, qualitative monotone claim: precision increases with averaging period; no numeric ratio given. Related reported benchmark from the same source: six empirical N-export models all predicted annual riverine N export from 16 northeastern US watersheds to within +/-50% of measured, with the flagship (SPARROW) calibrated on 374 watersheds - ~20x our 19 families, and an ANNUAL LOAD figure not comparable to our LOFO R2 0.328.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable / unknown (the 16-watershed evaluation may overlap SPARROW's 374-watershed calibration set)
sources: Peters, Reynolds & Johnes (2007), IAHS Publ. 309:63-73, https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/1778/1/001778Peters.pdf - TIER 3, UNVERIFIED
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The annual-exceedance-rate experiment is a 19-point regression - small, but it is a 19-point regression on a much less noisy target than a daily one, which is exactly the trade this finding proposes. Any SPARROW-style spatially-referenced source/attenuation regression must be flagged as evidence-based at n=374, not n=19.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES for the proposed fallback - a per-basin annual exceedance rate predicted from static attributes needs no local observations. The product would deliver a coarser output (expected violation days per year) alongside or instead of a daily probability, which may be the honest product for an ungauged pin.

datasets.name: EPA StreamCat + NHDPlus V2 accumulated basin attributes (the attribute inventory surfaced from the restore-2018 repository: baseflow index bfi, topographic wetness index twi, bedrock permeability bedperm, surficial geology soller, principal aquifers, hydrologic landscape regions hlr, physiographic province physio, Level-3 ecoregion ecol3, stream density strm_dens, sinuosity, flood_storage / nid_storage dam storage, STATSGO soil variables)
datasets.url: https://www.epa.gov/national-aquatic-resource-surveys/streamcat-dataset ; NHDPlus V2 at https://www.epa.gov/waterdata/get-nhdplus-national-hydrography-dataset-plus-data ; the exemplar attribute assembly is documented in https://github.com/scworland/restore-2018 (combine_all_vars.R, scibase/gage/all_gage_covariates.csv) with the underlying southeastern-US release at doi:10.5066/P9KXTDU4
datasets.resolution: NHDPlus V2 catchment (typically ~1-3 km2 local catchments), available both as local-catchment (Cat) and full-upstream-watershed-accumulated (Ws) values keyed by COMID
datasets.years: Static / long-term physiographic and geologic variables (no time dimension); land-cover-derived StreamCat layers exist for multiple NLCD epochs
datasets.access: Free public download - StreamCat bulk files and REST API; NHDPlus V2 via EPA/Horizon Systems bulk download. No authentication. The project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin and already uses USGS NLDI for on-the-fly delineation, so the COMID join key is in place.
datasets.license: US Government public domain / open (EPA and USGS products)
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - full CONUS coverage. This directly addresses the known inner-join defect where crop and N-surplus features silently UNDER-COUNT for basins extending outside Iowa, which is worst for the largest multi-state basins.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the angle's single most actionable output, and it is an INPUT fix rather than an output fix. Every duration-curve source that names which predictors carry the LEVEL of a site's distribution names subsurface and geologic descriptors - permeability, baseflow index, geology/soil indices - not weather scalars. That matches this project's own hard-won pattern (all wins came from geometry and static geography; nearly every hydrologically-motivated temporal feature failed). Baseflow index in particular is the closest available proxy for the missing tile-drainage control, since tile drainage alters the partition between quick and slow flow.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Join on the NHDPlus COMID already stored per basin (or resolve it from the NLDI delineation at prediction time), then create WATERSHED-ACCUMULATED (Ws) static features aggregated to the same three distance-from-outlet buckets already used for weather and CDL, so the schema does not change: bfi_ws_bucket{0,1,2} (area-weighted mean baseflow index over cells in each bucket), twi_ws_bucket{0,1,2} (area-weighted mean topographic wetness index), bedperm_ws_bucket{0,1,2} (area-weighted mean bedrock permeability class), plus whole-basin scalars soil_drainage_class_frac_welldrained, strm_dens_ws, sinuosity_ws, and one-hot or target-encoded hlr_dominant and ecol3_dominant. Use area-weighted means for continuous variables and area FRACTIONS for categorical ones (never modal class, which throws away the mixture that distinguishes basins). CRITICAL: use a LEFT join with explicit NaN accounting, not the current inner join, and add a coverage_fraction feature per bucket so the model can learn to distrust under-covered multi-state basins rather than silently seeing a biased mean.
datasets.limitations: Not verified in this research corpus - the attribute NAMES and their provenance in the Worland repository are verified (the verifier downloaded all_gage_covariates.csv and counted 5,736 rows x 48 columns), but the StreamCat/NHDPlus operational details above (exact URLs, current file layout, per-variable availability) were NOT independently checked and must be confirmed before acting. Sample-size warning: adding ~15 static features to a model with 19 independent basin families risks overfitting the between-site term you are trying to fix - add them in small named groups with LOFO evaluation after each group, never all at once. Finally, note the verified negative from Worland et al. (2019, doi:10.1029/2018WR024463): static basin characteristics were most informative for the LOW quantiles and least for the HIGH quantiles, and our target is an upper-tail exceedance - so temper expectations even for the right attributes.

datasets.name: USGS ScienceBase data release: 'Streamflow estimates for 74 streamgages in the Mobile-Tombigbee and Galveston-Trinity river basins using 16 estimation methods'
datasets.resolution: Daily, per streamgage; 74 sites x 3,653 days = 270,322 site-days; 16 method columns plus observed
datasets.access: Free public download from ScienceBase. NOTE: requires a browser User-Agent on curl - a bare curl or a markdown-fetch proxy returns 403 and produced the false conclusion that the work was inaccessible. Contains dv_output.csv (observed + all 16 method predictions), coord_input.csv (site coordinates and basin areas), and the complete R implementation (sb_main.R, sb_functions.R).
datasets.license: US Government public domain (USGS data release)
datasets.coversMultiState: Irrelevant - southeastern US only (Alabama/Mississippi and Texas). No Iowa coverage, no water-quality data.
datasets.whyUseful: NOT as input data. Useful only as a REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION: it is a working, readable codebase for the full QPPQ and copula method family, and it is the artifact that settles the transferability question without the paywalled PDF. Reading sb_functions.R is what reveals that the shipped configuration uses the target site's own empirical FDC and target-inclusive correlations - i.e. the partially-gaged case - which is the single fact that disqualifies this method family for our deployment target.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Do not incorporate as data. If anyone on the project proposes QPPQ or copula transfer, read sb_functions.R first and confirm which of the 16 methods are genuinely ungaged-capable (9 of 16: drainage-area-ratio, IDW, correlation-weighted and averaging variants) versus which require the target's own record (7 of 16, all the QPPQ_* and *_cop variants as archived). If a donor-channel experiment is run for Iowa nitrate, the inverse-distance-weighted nonexceedance transfer (QPPQ_IDW) is the simplest template - substitute nitrate percentiles from the k nearest monitored sensors for donor flow percentiles, and substitute an attribute-predicted nitrate concentration-duration curve for quantile(R[,i], ...), never the target's own.
datasets.limitations: Streamflow only, zero water-quality sites. Two dense contiguous nested networks (Mobile-Tombigbee median pairwise Spearman rho 0.774), so effective independent units are ~2 regions, not 74. Daily flow in humid southeastern basins is a poor analogue for nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa row crop. The truly-ungaged performance figures are NOT in this archive - they require the separate companion release doi:10.5066/P9YGKZZV.

datasets.name: Existing on-disk USGS discharge for 22 of 85 project sites
datasets.url: n/a - already present in the project's data directory; upstream source is USGS NWIS at https://waterservices.usgs.gov/
datasets.years: Up to 18 years per site, 0.66-0.97 record density
datasets.access: Already local; NWIS API is free, public, no authentication
datasets.coversMultiState: n/a - covers only the 22 gauged project sites. ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites have any discharge.
datasets.whyUseful: The ONLY way to test whether the duration-curve premise even holds for Iowa nitrate before investing in the machinery. With 22 gauged sites you can construct real flow-duration curves and real nitrate concentration-duration curves and measure two preconditions directly.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Run two cheap precondition tests, both on the 22-site subset. TEST 1 (does flow position explain nitrate?): for each of the 22 sites, assign every site-day to its EPA flow-duration zone (0-10% high, 10-40% moist, 40-60% mid, 60-90% dry, 90-100% low) using that site's own discharge record, then compute violation rate by zone within site. If violations do not concentrate strongly in the high/moist zones, the entire flow-duration framing is wrong for Iowa nitrate and the angle closes. TEST 2 (is the shape transferable and the level not?): fit a per-site nitrate concentration-duration curve, normalize each by its own median to separate level from shape, then check whether the normalized shapes cluster tightly across sites (the level/shape asymmetry the literature reports for streamflow) while the levels do not. Then, separately, regress the level parameter on static attributes under leave-one-family-out to get an honest estimate of whether the level is regionalizable at our n - this is the number that decides the angle.
datasets.limitations: 22 sites collapse to far fewer independent families under the project's own nesting rule, so both tests are underpowered and directional only. All 22 are USGS sites, which may not be representative of the 61 IWQIS sites that dominate the sensor network. And a positive result on the 22 does not establish that discharge can be regionalized to an ungauged pin - that remains a separate, unsolved problem for which no verified source in this corpus supplies a validated method or an error estimate.

refuted: REFUTED - 'Worland et al. (2019) trained multioutput neural networks on 688 USGS streamgages using 40 basin characteristics to predict 15 FDC quantiles, under a spatial holdout.' Four errors, one of them decisive. (a) PROTOCOL: NOT a spatial holdout. The authors' own code (scripts/Worland/remake_scripts/keras_funs.R, sw_k_foldcv) does random k=10 fold assignment over ROWS of a site-decade table with no grouping by site_no; each gage contributes up to 6 decade-rows with near-identical static attributes, so the same gage appears in train and test. The production model uses Keras validation_split=0.1 (last 10% of rows), also non-spatial. No leave-one-gage-out or PUB protocol appears anywhere in the neural-net path, and the 9,203 pour-point predictions are unvalidated extrapolation. Under project Rule 1 no number from this paper is comparable to LOFO 0.820. (b) 27 quantiles, not 15 - build_mnn_quantile.R and build_final_fdc_model.R define an explicit 27-element vector `f27` with `loss_weights <- c(rep(1,10), rep(1e-2,17))`; the 15-quantile version exists only in an abandoned June-2018 CloudML tuning script. (c) ~956 gages / ~2,804-2,816 gage-decades, not 688 - verified by downloading all_gage_covariates.csv (5,736 rows, 956 unique site_no x 6 decades) and all_gage_flow_stats.csv (2,804 rows, 956 unique site_no); the repo's own data/FactsAboutSiteLists.txt states 962 gages with a complete decade out of 1,290 screened. The figure 688 appears in no retrieved primary material. (d) '40 basin characteristics' is unconfirmed and may be a transcription artifact - 40 is also the width of the second hidden layer (`layer_dense(units = 40)`). NOTE the paper is not worthless: its abstract-verified directional finding (basin characteristics most useful for LOW quantiles, neighbouring-quantile bias terms most informative for HIGH quantiles) is a genuine negative for attribute-only upper-tail regionalization, and its attribute inventory is the best dataset lead in this angle. But it supplies no ungauged-transfer evidence.

REFUTED - 'Worland et al. (2019 copula paper) implies a data threshold on the order of years, not days, before target-site observations pay off, and the zero-observation deployment case sits below even the limited-data regime where the paper already finds no advantage.' Four grounds. (a) CATEGORY ERROR: abstract points (3) and (4) rank COPULAS AGAINST OTHER FDC-BASED METHODS within fixed information regimes; nothing compares a site's accuracy at N days of record versus zero. The pattern is fully consistent with all methods gaining large absolute skill from a short local record while their relative ordering converges. (b) The zero-observation case is NOT below the tested range - point (4) reads 'for ungaged sites AND partially gaged sites with limited data', so fully ungaged is explicitly one of the paper's two headline regimes. (c) 'Competitive albeit nondominating' is not 'no advantage'; it is a neutral-to-mildly-positive result for zero-observation regionalization, and the claim reverses the sign of the reported conclusion. (d) DROPPED CONDITIONAL: point (4) attributes the loss of dominance to 'when realistic error is introduced in the estimation of FDCs and correlations across the gaging network' - an injected-error condition, not record length alone. WHAT SURVIVES: quantile mapping and a fitted per-site random intercept genuinely cannot run at a pin with zero observations - but that is true by arithmetic, follows from the deployment definition, and citing this paper as its authority is a misattribution.

CORRECTED (not fully refuted) - 'no numeric results are extractable from Worland et al. 2019 WRR 10.1029/2019WR025138; obtain the PDF through a library.' The access failure is real and was reproduced independently (Wiley returns 403 with cf-mitigated: challenge on direct curl and 402 through a fetch proxy, on the landing page, /full, /epdf, /pdfdirect and /full-xml, despite a CC-BY license; OpenAlex lists exactly one OA location with no repository mirror; pubs.usgs.gov returns the abstract but its only content link points back to doi.org, so USGS hosts no PDF and that route is permanently dead, not transiently blocked). But the conclusion 'no numeric results extractable / split protocol not-applicable' is wrong: the companion data release doi:10.5066/P92F1ROU is fully public with a browser User-Agent and ships observed plus all 16 method predictions for 270,322 site-days, so method-level skill is directly recomputable, and the design is leave-one-site-out donor exclusion, not 'not-applicable'. GENERAL LESSON: when a publisher blocks a paper, resolve the companion USGS/ScienceBase data-release DOI before declaring the numbers unavailable.

CORRECTED - 'the 74 gages are ~4x more independent units than our n=19.' Apples-to-oranges and directionally backwards. Our 19 is a POST-COLLAPSE leak-safe count derived from 85 raw sites; Worland's 74 is a RAW gage count with no deduplication. Raw-to-raw, Iowa's 85 is the LARGER network. The 74 sit in only two HUC4s with heavy nesting (basin areas spanning ~15.7 to ~47,698 km2, a ~3,000x range) and measured pairwise Spearman rho with a Mobile-Tombigbee median of 0.774, 42% of pairs above 0.8, max 0.984. Applying our own nesting rule would collapse 74 to well below 19, and the study fits and evaluates each basin separately, so the effective number of independent regionalization units is closer to 2. This is NOT a small-n existence proof for QPPQ.

CORRECTED - 'method ranking REVERSES between the perfect-information and realistic-error regimes.' The abstract supports demotion from dominance to parity, not inversion: copulas move from 'outperform other methods' to 'competitive albeit nondominating', no competitor is reported to overtake them, and the abstract separately credits copulas with providing 'a hedge against poor performance when donor information becomes sparser and less informative' - i.e. relatively MORE robust as information degrades. Use 'the copula advantage collapses from dominance to parity'. Also: the realistic-error regime is confounded with record availability (result 4 covers ungaged AND limited-record partially gaged jointly), so it is not a clean single-axis information-quality manipulation.

CORRECTED - 'the binding constraint is the accuracy of the regionalized duration curve itself, not the dependence model.' Not established. The abstract degrades BOTH the FDCs AND the inter-site rank correlations simultaneously and never decomposes which drives the loss of dominance; the rank-correlation field IS the copula's dependence model, and at an ungaged site it must itself be regionalized. The defensible version: the limiting factor is the regionalization step as a whole. This strengthens rather than weakens the practical conclusion, since at an arbitrary pin we have realistic error in both inputs at once.

CORRECTED - 'this paper is evidence that the correct architecture is to keep rest_of_state_nitrate_lag* as the timing channel.' Unsupported and arguably backwards. A copula donor channel is site-specific and similarity-weighted; a single statewide scalar mean identical for every target pin is its DEGENERATE COLLAPSE. Read properly the paper suggests REPLACING the statewide mean with distance/attribute-weighted donor selection. Downgrade from 'evidence that the correct architecture is X' to 'a mathematical framing that motivates trying a separate concentration-duration-curve head, with that head's regionalization still facing the unchanged n=19 constraint.' Also correct the provenance: QPPQ predates this paper (Fennessey 1994; Hughes & Smakhtin 1996; Archfield & Vogel 2010) - Worland et al. generalize it, they do not define it.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE ABOUT A SOURCE - Peters, Reynolds & Johnes (2007, IAHS Publ. 309:63-73) contains ZERO mention of QPPQ, flow-duration curves, concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, quantile mapping, quantile regression, hierarchical/Bayesian partial pooling, random effects, or domain adaptation, verified against the complete extracted text; its 21-item reference list is entirely empirical-regression, mass-balance and critical-loads literature (SPARROW, FAB, export coefficient models). Anyone citing it as support for the level/shape-decomposition or duration-curve angle is citing it incorrectly. It remains a legitimate (tier-3) source for the aggregation-timescale argument and for the Nolan and McLay summaries.

REPORTED NEGATIVE ABOUT THE CANONICAL SOURCE (tier 3, unverified) - the IAHS/PUB duration-curve chapter is reported to contain NO treatment of concentration-duration curves, load-duration curves, TMDL practice, or any water-quality constituent (one passing citation, Bonta & Cleland 2003, JAWRA 39(6):1481-1496, doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2003.tb04433.x, named as the entry point), to never use the term 'QPPQ' at all, and to report zero hierarchical/Bayesian mixed-model or random-intercept regionalisation and zero quantile-regression-forest or distributional-GBDT work. If verified, this confirms both that the water-quality duration-curve literature is genuinely underused AND that the canonical streamflow synthesis will not supply it.
uncovered: HIERARCHICAL / BAYESIAN PARTIAL POOLING WITH SITE RANDOM INTERCEPTS PREDICTED FROM BASIN ATTRIBUTES - the assignment named this explicitly as a 'good answer' component and the corpus returned NOTHING. Not one paper, not at tier 1 and not at tier 3. The canonical duration-curve synthesis is reported (unverified) to contain zero such work. This is an absence of search, not an absence of evidence: the mixed-model / multilevel literature on regionalizing catchment properties exists and was simply not reached. Given that partial pooling is the standard statistical answer to 'estimate a level for a group with few or no observations, shrunk toward an attribute-predicted mean', and that it degrades gracefully at small n in a way a neural network does not, THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT UNRESEARCHED BRANCH OF THE ANGLE and should be re-run as its own search before the angle is closed.

QUANTILE REGRESSION FORESTS AND DISTRIBUTIONAL GBDT - the assignment asked specifically for these options and the corpus contains NOTHING on quantile regression forests, NGBoost, natural-gradient boosting, LightGBM/XGBoost quantile or multiquantile objectives, or CatBoost multiquantile, in any hydrological or water-quality application. Zero sources at any tier. This is a complete gap and is particularly conspicuous because the project already uses XGBoost, so a distributional objective would be a low-friction change requiring no new data.

DOMAIN ADAPTATION - named in the research question, zero coverage at any tier. No CORAL, no adversarial domain adaptation, no importance weighting, no covariate-shift correction, nothing on transfer between monitored and unmonitored catchments framed as a domain-adaptation problem. Not searched.

CONCENTRATION-DURATION CURVES FOR NITRATE OR ANY WATER-QUALITY CONSTITUENT - no source in the corpus, verified or unverified, constructs or regionalizes a concentration-duration curve. The entire verified evidence base for this angle is STREAMFLOW. The extension from flow-duration curves to nitrate concentration-duration curves is this project's own analogy and is completely untested in the retrieved literature.

ANY WATER-QUALITY APPLICATION OF QPPQ - searched and not found. The only water-quality duration-curve material in the corpus is the descriptive Kamrath & Yuan load partitioning (tier 3, no transfer model) and the EPA TMDL guidance (tier 3, prescriptive, zero validation). The load-duration-curve literature IS underused as the assignment hypothesized, but the corpus establishes that the canonical streamflow source will not supply it - Bonta & Cleland (2003, JAWRA 39(6):1481-1496, doi:10.1111/j.1752-1688.2003.tb04433.x) is named as the entry point and was NEVER RETRIEVED. That is a specific, cheap follow-up.

NUMERIC EFFECT SIZES FROM WORLAND ET AL. (2019, doi:10.1029/2019WR025138) - no NSE, KGE, RMSE or bias figure from the paper itself could be verified through any free route. Wiley's Cloudflare block is a bot challenge, not a licensing paywall, on a CC-BY article, so a human with a browser would likely obtain the PDF; that remains the correct next step if the numbers are ever needed. Partial mitigation: method-level skill is recomputable from the companion data release, but only for the partially-gaged configuration.

TRULY-UNGAGED PERFORMANCE FIGURES FOR THE COPULA/QPPQ FAMILY - genuinely absent from the archived data release. The ungaged variant requires kriged correlations plus neural-net-regionalized FDCs from a second release (doi:10.5066/P9YGKZZV, 9,203 HUC12 pour points, southeastern US, 1950-2009), and its performance figures were not located. So the corpus contains NO verified quantitative estimate of how well any duration-curve transfer method performs at a genuinely zero-observation site.

HOW A DURATION CURVE IS ACTUALLY REGIONALIZED FROM ATTRIBUTES, AT TIER 1 - this was named in the assignment as a 'good answer' component and no VERIFIED source supplies it. The only operational recipes in the corpus are tier-3 (the IAHS chapter's reported index-flow/parametric two-stage approach: fit a distribution per gauged site, then regress its parameters on attributes; reportedly Castellarin et al. 2007 predicted a logistic position parameter representing mean annual runoff from area and mean annual net precipitation, and a kappa position parameter representing within-year variability from catchment permeability and elevation range; reportedly Li et al. 2010 found catchment area and geographic location NOT sufficiently explanatory for FDC shape, which is a caution against this project's reliance on lat/lon as top-ranked features; reportedly the chapter summarizes that 'Geology or geology/soil related indices and topographic elevation ... are the most frequently used predictors of the slope/shape of FDCs, in addition to the aridity index, which governs the mean'). ALL UNVERIFIED. The verified sources describe the decomposition but never the regionalization step - which is precisely the step this project needs.

PROJECTED SKILL FOR AN ATTRIBUTE-PREDICTED LEVEL AT n=19 - no source, at any tier, in any domain, reports out-of-sample skill for regionalizing a distributional level parameter from a training set of ~19 independent units. The closest reported precedents are n=13 in-sample (Kamrath & Yuan, unverified, no holdout) and n=88 apparently in-sample (McLay, unverified). This is the number that would actually decide the angle, and it does not exist in the literature - which means the only way to get it is the cheap internal experiment described under the on-disk discharge dataset: regress a per-family level parameter on static attributes under leave-one-family-out and measure it directly.

IOWA-SPECIFIC OR TILE-DRAINED-MIDWEST DURATION-CURVE WORK - nothing. Every verified source is southeastern US humid/subtropical streamflow; the closest tier-3 material is Ohio (Kamrath & Yuan, 14 watersheds) and an Illinois nitrate figure in EPA guidance. No source addresses artificially tile-drained agricultural hydrology, which is the known dominant control in Iowa and remains absent from the feature set with no data source identified.
